utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before the witness will be invited to enter the courtroom, we'll first move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I also announce that we'll have the second session of this morning to be a little bit shorter. We'll have an early break at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again remind that you you're still bound by the declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony and Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to start, Your Honours, by responding to a query raised yesterday, Your Honour, with respect to 65 ter number 33333, and in fairness to Mr. Poparic, I'd like to do it in front of him. If we could see that photograph. Your Honours' query was whether we could assist with the direction from which this photograph was taken, and ... just by way of a reminder to everybody, and -- this is the photograph we were discussing yesterday, 65 ter number 33333. Now if we could go to the image that's in P3, which is our court book, page 16 [Microphone not activated]. Sorry. E-court page 20. E-court page 20. Hard copy page 16; e-court page 20. Now -- thank you. Now this 65 ter number was -- is a still taken from a video-clip which has also been separately uploaded and can be reverted to if there's a need. But, Your Honours, this photograph was taken from that part of the complex of the school for the blind, which is the building sitting at the south-west corner of the hexagon which encompasses the school for the blind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the school for the blind is the long building at the north-east building of the hexagon, if I'm describing that clearly enough, and this still was taken from a clip that was filmed from the building in the south-west corner at the shortest end of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that ... and that road on which we find the red car is a road which is invisible because it is hidden by the buildings themselves on the other photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is, indeed. But if we were to play the clip that this was created from, which I can just refer to now and we can play if there's a need, you are able to clearly see that road as we look out the windows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just, again, for the record, that -- the image comes from 65 ter number 33269 and a clip from time code 8:06 to about 8:16 makes clear that this is one and the same road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could -- if it's only ten seconds, perhaps we look at it so we are certain that our present understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we'll just start at time code 8:06 of 65 ter number 33269, and this is without the sound, this whole video. We're not relying on the sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, you see that road from about 8:09 to 8:14. And, of course, we can play a longer clip, if there's a need. And we ended at time code 8:16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask, if I may, that this clip that we've just played from 65 ter number -- that this clip we just played be tendered as the next Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 33269 receives exhibit number P7605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And admission will be decided upon once the video-clip has been provided to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, what I'd like to do now that we've dispensed with this for the time being is come back to the pictures I promised you yesterday, and we were talking about the building of the school for the blind. Now, when -- what you pointed out in commenting on this photograph was that you can see the building in Djura Jaksic with a red facade and that the garage was, from this location, an obstacle to the specific F-9 incident location. So what I wanted to do is show you some progression from the south-western building, where this photo was taken from, to the building that appeared in your report as image 122 and 120 and the basis for image 123. Now, so what I'd like to us do is look at 65 ter number 26173A, please. So here's a photograph, Mr. Poparic, taken on 12 October 2000 from the building that appears in 65 ter number 32782, which we saw briefly yesterday and in your report. And this can be broadcast. And in your report at image 122 and 123. So it was taken from that building from the furthermost window according to the description I have on the right, room 63 on the top floor as you approach the building from the direction of the intersection. Now, this photograph shows a clear and unobstructed line of sight to the incident location for F-9, doesn't it? We can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never disputed that there is a part of the building from which there is a view.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 26173A receives exhibit number P7606, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this -- this is the photograph without telephoto that was the basis for the image that is in the court binder of the incident location as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, so here's my question related to this and the line of sight. In your testimony in-chief, you remember we watched a part of an exhibit, video-clip, and it's called P1934, and it was where the witness -- a clip where the witness showed where she and her girlfriend were standing at the time her girlfriend was shot. Now, that position is what you marked yesterday in -- I'll just look to get the number for a moment. P7604.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right, the arrow that you marked there, you said was the incident location; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look at image 128 in your report, which is English page 176 and B/C/S page 172.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the report is D1330, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we only need -- because the question is about the image, so we only need one image and you could blow it up. Now you talked about this image in your testimony in-chief, and you said at transcript page 40491 that Medina Omerovic and Sanela Muratovic were in the street Djura Jaksica roughly at the spot marked number 5 on this image. Those two locations aren't the same. Can you see that right? The spot that you marked at number 5, where you said the witness said she was, and the spot you marked yesterday aren't the same? You can see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are different places.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, if you go and put your image 125 and your image 128 side by side --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we've got here 128 on the screen and you said in your report that the incident site for F-9 was marked at number 1. So -- and here's image 128 on the right-hand side, so you're even -- this shows you're even internally inconsistent. You've marked two different incident locations and, in fact, neither of them are where the witness said the victim was when she was shot; right? You can see that.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you not see that neither of these images accurately mark where the victim showed us she was shot in the video-clip we watched in your testimony in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness asked for some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see it. You're right. This point 1 should have been moved to this intersection forward. 1 and 2 are shifted. It's the intersection between the buildings around point 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, sorry. I apologise. No, it's -- it's marked correctly. It's marked correctly. This point 1 is the red building on this picture 128, marked as 3. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your image 128 that you talked about in your testimony in-chief has number 5 marked incorrectly. You can see that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. On image 128, point 5 would correspond to point 2, would correspond to point 2 on image 125.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll ask this one more time by looking at one more picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we can back, please, to P3, hard copy page 18. I think it's e-court page 22. Actually, let me move forward a couple of pages. No, let's stay with that. Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The red circle in the image you see on the left-hand side is a marking that denotes where the witness said the victim was standing when she was shot. Your marking number 5 on your image 128 doesn't accurately represent where the victim said she was standing -- where the witness said the victim was when she was shot; right? You can see that: The two of them aren't the same; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct they're not the same. Point 5 is where the witness said they were when ABiH soldiers told them to hurry along because there is a danger of enemy fire. Somebody showed yesterday the statement of this girl who was wounded. She said that they were going from Senada Dindic number 1 where she lived to this building marked 3 at the corner. So from that direction they came to the intersection and then they were warned about the danger and that point 5 is approximately where the witness described they had been, and then they ran between buildings 2 and 3. So the circle on this image that you showed, from point 5 they came to that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I won't belabour this point. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- with respect to image 128? You describe in your report the spot number 5 as -- and perhaps we can move it a little bit to the left. The spot where Sanela Muratovic was at the time in question according to Medina Omerovic's statement and testimony. What do you mean by "the time in question"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant at the time of the incident if it is correctly translated. Let me see how it's defined here. No, no, that translation is not good. In the original it says the place where Sanela Muratovic was according to the statement and testimony of Medina Omerovic. No, it's good. It's good. I don't have the time in the original. I'm not -- I think it's not the best translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Number 5 is on the street near the intersection. In your understanding, was she -- wait -- wait a moment, please, before I finish my question. In your understanding, was she shot there or after moving in the direction to the right on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat how this girl described it. When they were approximately at that place, number 5, they were warned that there was a threat, and they started running. At that moment gun-fire was heard and in one statement Medina Omerovic says that's when Sanela Muratovic was shot and then they ran to the trench to get assistance from the soldiers. In my view, that incident is very probable because the traces on the buildings number 2 and number 3 from the front on this red brick, as well as the traces on these buildings marked as 4, indicate that there was a very intensive exchange of fire. You can see that also on building number 2. Building number 4 has been renovated but in my report there is also a picture that indicates the same. In my view, fire was opened from that direction and she was hit by a ricochet bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was a very long answer to a very short question. Can we scroll a little bit down, please. What you just said in explaining the photograph and your markings, I don't see -- oh, thank you. It is at least the description of number 5 it's not very clear in the English language. That's all that I want to say. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have two short follow-up questions. If you say they were there and they started running, et cetera, does that allow you to tell us exactly where they were when the one girl was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In my view, they probably don't know that either. Because it's dynamic, a dynamic process and they were hit somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of them was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say when one of them told Mr. Hogan when and where she was hit, she doesn't know actually because you, although not knowing where that exactly was, that you think that she's wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say what I know in terms of what she said. She said at one moment to Mr. Hogan that they were at the edge of the trench when the other one was hit, and I said that, that in the testimony she described it a bit differently. She said we ran and then fire was opened and then she was hit. Yesterday we saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the statement of the girl who had been hit and she is not saying that it was at the trench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that the evidence in this respect may be not fully consistent because what was said to Mr. Hogan may be a bit different from what was said in the statement. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a slight difference, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes. Is it within your expertise to tell us which is better to be believed than the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not make any recommendations in terms of what should be believed. I looked at both cases. The case when she was standing at the trench, would it be possible for her to be hit from the other direction, and I came to the conclusion that then there was no such possibility. Except that part of the window that we see, that the marksman was not up there. So he would have been somewhere around the middle of the window because -- and I excluded that because it's opposite BH army positions and, according to figure 123, we see that that's very dangerous for a person to be there and then on the basis of the rest, I concluded that it was not possible to do it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it was too dangerous, therefore, the marksman couldn't have been there. That's your position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is that the window is open. You see how big it is and I mean, I doubt -- well, I mean, at the time of combat, there was some fire there then and then it would be illogical for me to believe that during that combat he would come to the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have another question which is the following. You said due to the impacts, I understand bullet impacts on the various buildings, you concluded that there was an exchange of fire at that point in time. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that on the basis of these -- this enormous number of traces at number 2, 3 and 4, I came to the conclusion that during the war conflict in that area there was an intensive exchange of gun-fire between the warring parties and that is why I assume that fire could have been opened from that direction. So I don't know where the firing position was. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The traces show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The trace do not show anything about what happened on that day, at that hour, do they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not explicitly, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Implicitly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Implicitly, if we link up the first statement or, rather, the testimony of Medina Omerovic who says that she ran, I mean, and it would have been possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. My question was whether the traces do show anything about what happened on that day as far as exchange of fire is concerned at that specific time. You said no, not explicitly. Therefore, then I asked you whether they show anything implicitly. That is, the traces. I didn't ask you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Traces, no. Traces, no. So many traces. It would be pointless, I mean, to look for something there. They just give a general picture concerning the scene itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they do not say anything explicitly, neither implicitly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one small follow-up. By virtue of the marks that you see on the buildings, there was a exchange of fire. What evidence do you have to show that there was outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, take a look at photograph - sorry, I don't know it by heart - 120. 120. It's these buildings marked with number 4. This was a home for the elderly before the war and now it is a company --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can we just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 128. No, well, yeah. But in my report, photograph 120 shows the home for the elderly and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 120 is at page 167, e-court. English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. How do you -- what -- where's the evidence to show that there was outgoing fire? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see evidence on the facades of these buildings. You see how many hits there are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, is that outgoing fire or incoming fire. Is that evidence of incoming fire or is that evidence of outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is evidence that fire was incoming for these four, that's to say, there was shooting from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. I'm asking what evidence do you have that there was outgoing fire. That is incoming fire. Oh. In the opposite direction. Because there was an exchange of fire, according to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For outgoing fire, it's building number 2 and picture 128. And it is shown here. Part of that building is on 119. It was hit in many places and that is to say that that fire had come from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what you're saying. If the house -- the building is hit and you say it's hit by fire that comes from there? I am looking at number 2, picture 128. If it is hit, it's hit by incoming fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. In picture 120, incoming fire is from building marked as number 2 in image 128. Whereas, in picture 119, incoming fire is from building 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have picture 119 on the screen now. You asked for 120. Now there's 119.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see? The facade was repaired a bit, but the traces are still there. Incoming fire is from this direction that I marked as A, roughly, but basically it's the area of this building number 4 that we saw in picture 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. This whole discussion is about whether there would have been fire during the war. Does that got anything to do specifically with the date and the time of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me ask you: If we look at a wall with a lot of bullet damage, what tells us that it was on that date that the two girls were there that this damage was inflicted, or was it inflicted somewhere during the war time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we could not say anything about a concrete day but the volume of damage indicates that it certainly must have been over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But that doesn't allow for any conclusions on an exchange of fire on that day, would it? It would only allow for a conclusion that there must have been, at one point in time during the war or during a longer period of time in the war, such exchange of fire which would have caused that damage. That's, I think, the only conclusion that you could draw, or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do not agree fully because if we look at the situation here on the ground, there is no denying that fire had been opened and there was testimony to that effect so it only could have come from this direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so, but now you are moving away from my question. My question was: What can you seen and what can be concluded on that photograph, if fire was opened on that day that might explain possibly, one, two, three, or five bullet-holes, if they hit a building at all, nothing more, nothing less. So therefore showing a huge impact of exchange of fire on a building is hardly to be related logically to this incident? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These traces cannot help us establish whether the projectile hit the building that day in one spot or another spot. We cannot do that because there's a large number. But as we look at these traces and the surrounding buildings, we can conclude that during the war there was an exchange of gun-fire in that direction. We do not have any traces elsewhere. So if it was opened on that day, that is to be expected. Now that's my position. Then, we can expect that fire had been opened from that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can -- may I put one additional question. Do you have any evidence that, on that day, at that time, when this woman was hit, a single shot was fired from or nearby the place where she was hit? Do you have any evidence to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No evidence as to where the bullet was fired from. Nobody said anything about that. Only a gun-shot was heard, so it's only the sound that was heard that is evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How can you then say that at the time of the incident that there was exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the statement of this girl, that soldiers had warned them and that shooting had started. That's what they said. So soldiers warned them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I stop you. Did the girl say anything about outgoing fire from that position? Where they were hit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't. And I don't think that they could have concluded anything. They heard this sound and, of course, they were afraid. They ran away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you have no evidence about exchange of fire. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for clarification, what Judge Fluegge specifically pointed at, that exchange of fire is fire coming from both sides; whereas, all of your answers seems to focus on shots being fired not necessarily from two sides but could be from one side as well. I just clarified my understanding of the question and your answers so that if there's any further reason to comment you have the possibility, but I first leave it in the hands of Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, you have clarified. I am satisfied with that. "Exchange" means exchange and not one-side fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if you have clear evidence that it came from two sides, you may explain that. But all your answers, until now, has not pointed at that. If you want to be focussed on that, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not claiming that the girl was hit by BH army fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All my analyses show that it is a ricochet from incoming fire so it doesn't have to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, you are dealing with a matter different from what I raised during my question and giving you an opportunity to further comment. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move onto another incident now. And it's the unscheduled incident you deal with in paragraphs 247 to 252 of your report and it's the sniping death of Adnan Kasapovic on 24 October 1994 and it also deals with the school for the blind. Now, the way I understand your argument in respect of this incident is that because some trees which you claimed were evergreen were there during the war, they would have blocked the line of sight between the school for the blind and the incident location, and you said that at paragraph 250. So I'd like to look at a photo we saw yesterday; 65 ter number 32782, please. Now am I also correct in understanding based on what I read in your report that your only source for that assertion is what you see in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I dealt with this incident because Mr. Van der Weijden dealt with that incident and he claimed that there was excellent visibility so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question was whether you exclusively relied on what you see in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I have this photograph admitted as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which photograph? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter 32783, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that would receive, Madam Registrar, number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P7607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you have no idea whether there might be a line of sight to the incident location from positions elsewhere in buildings in the compound of the school for the blind, do you? You have no idea; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deal with that. I just indicated that Mr. Van der Weijden did not take into account this fact that there's a tree there. At the time when he visited, it wasn't there, so he didn't know about this, so that was the only thing that was the subject of my observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered my question. I'd like now to go on to another unscheduled incident, one you dealt with, which is your unscheduled incident 9 from your Annex 6, and it's paragraphs 41 to 52 in your Annex 6. I think pages 327 to 334 in your language; and 346 to 353 in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for this to appear, Madam Registrar would like to correct something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P7607 was assigned to the 65 ter number 32782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now let's go to image 36 of your report which is, I think, on page 350 in English, and I think, B/C/S page 330. So you know -- and we only need, frankly, one picture. You know that this image which is for some reason I should say, labelled as image 41 in B/C/S but image 36 in English. You know that this image does not show the same room that the victim in this case, Enes Pasic, was shot in, does it? You know that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that is what is shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Poparic, you know that the flat that Enes Pasic was shot in faced west, and you know that the flat shown in this photo which you used is on the opposite side of the building with the balcony facing east. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It doesn't change anything in my findings. These are completely identical apartments. I just looked at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this is an apartment facing the east, whereas Mr. Pasic's apartment was facing the west, but the apartments are identical, and I just put this in here to show what apartments are like in this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But facing east or west may be relevant, isn't it? Because even if the layout of the flat is the same, the orientation is 180 degrees different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. And I worked on that basis. I'm very familiar with this because I lived in an apartment like that 100 metres away and I had a friend in that building who had an apartment like this. I know this perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that doesn't change east and west, whether you lived there, how many friends you had living there, east is east and west is west. They're not the same. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you know that from the buildings of the school for the blind, that complex encircled by the red hexagon that we saw in the photo in P3 earlier this morning, you know that's a clear and unobstructed line of sight from those buildings to the building where Enes Pasic's apartment faces west. You know his apartment is exposed to potential firing positions from the buildings of the school for the blind; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that you know that and I accepted that and I analysed the incident from that aspect, and I was not denying that there was visibility in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have the English version of the description of photograph 41 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, the description is on the immediately preceding page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see here now the indication image 36, as you said, it must be an error, the numbering and it says the living-room in the flat of Djordja Andrejevica Kuna Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Edgerton is drawing our attention to the previous page, the beginning of paragraph 49, which I think is related to what we see here. Could we move to the previous page, after now having read the title of the image. 49 reads: "Image 36 shows the living-room where Enes Pasic was." Is that a mistake, Witness, because it shows a similar living room, although differently oriented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably a mistake. Let me see. That's 49; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just read it to you. Because from your previous answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. It's a mistake in the translation here. In my original, it says image 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Image 41. So let's then have a look at the original. Ms. Edgerton, I take it that you know the page in the original. I haven't prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The page in the original B/C/S should be page 350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at that. Yes. But, Witness, I mean, there may be a reference to image 41, but the -- image 41 in the original is the same as image 36 in the English version. So, therefore, the reference remains unchanged. And I do understand that you -- what you wanted to say is that this was a living-room similar to the one in which Enes Pasic was and that the title of the image itself should be the living-room in a flat, not the flat, in the street mentioned. Are these the mistakes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the caption approximately. The living-room in a flat in Djordja Andrejevica Kuna Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a living-room, not necessarily the living Enes Pasic was in. As a matter of fact, not the room he was in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's just an apartment that was for sale and I took it from the real estate agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to read paragraph 49 on the left side on the screen to clarify what you really wrote there. Just that one line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The aspect of the living-room where Enes Pasic was is given in image 41. This is a bit misleading. The orientation is not good on this image but it's correct on the sketches that I provided, on the basis of which I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You would have said that at the beginning of this line of questioning, that this is misleading and that this is the mistake, we should -- we wouldn't have wasted so much time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see we're past the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we have to take a break. We'll take a break. And, Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go on to another incident that you dealt at English page 146 and B/C/S page 144 of your report in paragraphs 114 to 132. And it's an incident in which two women were shot and wounded in their legs while travelling in a crowded bus near the junction of Nikola Demonja and Bulevar Avnoj, presently Nikola Demonja and Bulevar branilaca Dobrinje in Dobrinja and it happened on 25 May 1994. Now you're not disputing that these two women were shot and wounded, are you, Sehadeta Plivac and Hajra Hafisovic? You agree that happened.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also agree that there were VRS firing positions in the faculty of theology in Nedzarici, don't you? You don't dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny that, except that firing position was looking in another direction, not towards Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What then is your knowledge of the firing positions upon which you base this assertion? Were you there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there during the war, but during my tour of that faculty, I believe the rector of the faculty, that man was, who offered us photographs made after the reintegration of that area and he allowed us to copy these photographs because it's very clear from these images where the firing positions were around the faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And let's talk about firing positions a bit more before we get to direction. Are you prepared to accept that these firing positions were manned with anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I saw on the photographs, hardly. Perhaps in some other place but on that building the opening was too small, if I was able to estimate it correctly from the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've not seen any military documents, I take it, then, that might affect your position as to there were anti-aircraft guns at the faculty of theology; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any documents. I know there was a tank around there. There was a garage inside the kitchen, that was shown to me as well, but I don't know which weapons were there. I don't have any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Retire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could I see clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked whether you are prepared to accept that these firings positions were manned with anti-aircraft guns and then you said according to what I saw in the photographs, hardly. Now, not having been there and looking at the photographs alone I imagine that it is difficult to say whether they were there or not there, but do you allow for the possibility that these firing positions were manned with anti-aircraft guns? Because I'm a bit puzzled by your "hardly."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allow the possibility that there were anti-aircraft guns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you've answered my question. But you think it may not have been very likely, if I understood you well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, could we please see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, excuse me, if I may clarify. I'm talking about the firing positions that I saw on top of the building. It's in image 105. I'm talking only about them, not about everything that was around the theological faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at 65 ter number 33219.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now this document is dated 11 August 1993. You'll see it when it appears. And it's an Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina enemy assessment marked strictly confidential, and it's from the -- on the last page, from the assistant Chief of Staff for intelligence and security. Now at English and B/C/S page 1, paragraph 3, the last sentence in this document reports with respect to the aggressors we see at the top of paragraph 3. "In the Trapera sector, in the sixth house, in the second row, a PAM is positioned, while machine-gun nests are found on the church and in the grove below the church in the houses below the Bijelo Polje road, Ikic houses, the theology building, the Nedzarici barracks" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "The Nedzarici barracks and near the Aleksa Santic school." So here's a document, contemporaneous document, from almost a year before the incident that says there's a machine-gun nest at the theology building; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it says machine-gun, he doesn't mean the anti-aircraft gun, PAM. This term means --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as machine-gun, it's usually M74 or M54.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I asked you what the document says. This -- can you confirm that this is a contemporaneous document that says a year before the incident, there's a machine-gun nest at the theology building.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it's a contemporaneous document and that there was a machine-gun nest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're prepared to accept that there was a machine-gun nest at the faculty of theology; right? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. And now I can say that based on the appearance of the building, it's possible that there was a machine-gun. Before that, I said I could not --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- be convinced that it was an anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this part of document or whole document? What is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know? It's -- Ms. Edgerton, perhaps you could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have explained on the record, I thought quite clearly what it was, Your Honours. An ABiH document dated the 11th of August, 1993, and I'm just repeating myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in e-court, it's eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, there are authentication details that are uploaded as part of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the question is do you want the entire eight pages admitted or do you want just this page. I guess this is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am asking is this the entire document because there's nothing on the first page, and it says page 9, as I can see on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there is no date only, although this is typewritten document, probably my learned friend is quoting the date from the last page written in handwriting. So that's why I'm asking what this document is all about. Who composed and how can we know who composed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps where does it come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where does it come from, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we go over to B/C/S page 2, and I'm not sure off the top of my head which English page that might be, we can see exactly where the document comes from. And.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That should be page 2 in English as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think so. One would hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this document comes from the archives of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's certified as being authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Doesn't that mean that are you tendering the two pages we have looked at?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the whole document, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what's on the rest because I see that page 3 in e-court starts with the page numbering 2, which raises some questions as where that page 1 comes from or whether -- no, let me just have a look. I think I see it now what happens. I think the -- what seems to be the situation, if I look at it, is that we have, first, a page; then we have a short page with -- an attestation where it comes from; then we have another page, which is then page 2, though page 3 in e-court, which is then followed again by such an attestation; the same is true for page 5, which is page 3. At least that's what we find on the top of that page. And on page 6 we find the attestation that it comes from the archives. So, in effect, if I could cut matters short, apparently we are talking about a three-page document which, for each page, an attestation where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's also puzzling for us, Your Honour. Why do attestation for every page? There is -- there must be, then, the whole document, or we -- I don't know. But usually attestation is given to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is the question now about the practice of the archives in the military archives in attesting to every page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The question is, first of all, the structure of the document. It was unclear to us at the very beginning. I think that has been cleared now. And I think -- is that a question or is that an objection to admission, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's an objection. We cannot see source. We cannot see who composed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's another matter. And then you said something about the date as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date we can find only on the original because of these attestations pages on the second-last page entered by hand and we don't know whether it is entered at the time when the document was composed or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at that. I take it that you are looking at page 5 in e-court in the B/C/S original?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we look at that. You say what we find at the bottom there --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Than seems to read: 11.08.93 and then .g, which I think often stands for "godine," which is date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, and Ms. Edgerton quoted this date as the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton, these questions. Apparently in support of an objection to admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is in interests of time for a very long cross-examination is move on and come back to Your Honours with a submission on this, please, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But should the document be MFI'd meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we can keep track of it, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 33219 is marked as P7608.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another document, 65 ter 33218. And it's a document dated 12 October 1993. And it's an intelligence report from the 5th Motorised Brigade Command to the 1st Corps Command intelligence organ. Let's go over to English page 2 and B/C/S page 3, please, the last sentence of paragraph 2. It says -- and it's just above the heading of paragraph 3 at the bottom of the English page. Oh, your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This says: "A 120-millimetre mortar platoon and an 82-millimetre mortar battery are located by the faculty of theology and there is an 82-millimetre mortar platoon on the old Butmir road leading to the airport. PATs are deployed in the faculty of theology in Nedzarici." A PAT is a 20-millimetre anti-aircraft gun, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it has an effective range of 2500 metres; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your report on this incident you said, in paragraph 30, that the distance between the faculty of theology and the incident site in this case amounted to 1527 metres. Now, not accepting your distance measurements for a moment as being accurate, you claimed that the weapons used by the VRS didn't have the technical capacities -- capabilities required for taking aim and firing at distances of 1527 metres. This document, this contemporaneous military document, confirms that weapons capable of hitting a bus at 1500 metres were actually deployed at the faculty of theology, doesn't it? You're contradicted.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, PAT was certainly able to hit at 1500 metres. However, the traces on the bus and the injuries exclude the possibilities that the fire was from a PAT.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask you that. You said -- you said that the VRS, the weapons used by the VRS didn't have the technical capabilities required for taking aim and firing at distances of 1500 metres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you point us exactly where in the report this is it stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 130. I think earlier we were -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we see that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we take this document away, I would just -- one -- put one correction on the transcript. Ms. Edgerton, you quoted from the last paragraph before number 3 and said: "PATs are deployed at the faculty of theology in Nedzarici," but there is one word missing, the word "and." It should read "in the faculty of theology and in Nedzarici."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so. Thank you. I'm always happy to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do we have on our screens paragraph 130. No, we don't have it --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English page 153, is what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether in view of the document just shown to you, whether you accept that the weapons used could cover such a distance of 1527 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by what I said in my report. Because all the evidence indicates that the bus was hit from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not talking about the bus. I'm just -- there may be many reasons to still support your conclusions, but the one and only matter which is asked at this moment is whether you stand by what you say in paragraph 130. I'm not talking about any of the other paragraphs. You may be fully right. But whether you still take the view that the weapons used by the VRS members did not have the technical capabilities required for taking aim and firing at these distances; that's 1527 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by it completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was just put to you by Ms. Edgerton that there was at least a report which says that there was a PAT at the theology faculty which you said would cover 2500 metres. Could you explain why you still think that where such a weapon which was reported to be there could cover 2500 metres, why the weaponry used by the VRS could not cover 1527 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I maintained that based on the evidence gathered on the spot about the damage to the bus and the injuries sustained. Second of all -- it is not an infantry weapon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not talking about the bus. The only thing I'm talking about - and I give a last opportunity to answer that question - is whether in view of what was put to you a minute ago by Ms. Edgerton, whether you still think, apart from any bus or whatever incident, that the weaponry of the VRS at the theology faculty could not cover or strike at the distance of 1527 metres. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant infantry weapons. A PAT is a cannon. It's not an infantry weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 130, you say "the weapons used by the VRS members did not have the technical capabilities required for taking aim and firing at these distances." It doesn't limit itself to whatever kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm limiting myself to the weapons that were there, the small-arms, whereas a PAT is an anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Again, you have missed the opportunity to answer my question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the next paragraph talks about the specific weapon, 7.62-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not talking about the incident, I was just talking about 130, paragraph 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was discussing this incident so we cannot talk about guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's -- no objections at this moment. This is debate, argument, rather than anything else. Ms. Edgerton is invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a Praga, if I pronounce it correctly or Praga gun is a 30-millimetre anti-aircraft gun; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that has an effective range of 2.000 metres at ground targets, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a maximum range of 3 and a half kilometres; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you please have a look at the transcript. If one of the previous pages -- questions is correct. The effective range of 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 2.000 metres. Rather than 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, in theory, a Praga, at a distance of 1500 metres from a bus would have been perfectly capable of piercing it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we'll -- as I said, we'll have a short session. At this moment, we'll conclude in one or two minutes. I don't know whether have you any follow-up questions or whether you wanted to move to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Either one would take more than one or two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we first take a break. And then most likely, and I must stress that - the Chamber will resume at ten minutes to 12.00 but then in a composition of two Judges, because I'm unable to sit and my colleagues will decide whether they consider it in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I then just ask one thing before we rise, Your Honours. Could I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need the witness for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then, the witness is already excused. And we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think he may not have been -- and it was simply to have 65 ter number 33218 marked as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33218 receives exhibit number P7609, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I had one thing but perhaps there's a follow-up after the break which I will not -- which I'll have to read then later on. You spent a lot of time on demonstrating that the one room wasn't the other one. I expected more in the follow-up, how would that have impacted or influenced the conclusions, but nothing followed. That's something, of course, because if it has no impact, then it's something which is not, perhaps, accurate but without any consequences, and I wonder whether we should spend that much time if it does not affect the conclusions. Mr. Lukic, as far as the Defence is concerned, I think we -- or at least the firing tables for the -- at least firing tables without a translation for modified air bombs as they were presented, was given but nothing further happened with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we sent it for translation, and we are actually applying, I think, to get the full versions of both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of both firing tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... have a follow-up or not. The only thing relevant for this witness is that he brought these excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that means they are there now. We'll take a break, and my colleagues will resume at ten minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness may please come in. As indicated before the break, the two of us have agreed to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As soon as the witness comes in, you may proceed, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poparic, still talking about the faculty of theology, in point of fact, the location was heavily militarised during the war with machine-guns, with anti-aircraft guns, with heavy calibre anti-aircraft guns, with mortars, and that's confirmed by the documents.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not challenging that. I said there was a tank too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, another leg of your argument with respect to this incident is that from the school of theology the place is invisible, and you said in your testimony in-chief at transcript page 40350 that you couldn't take a photograph because of the crown of a tree. So I'd like us to just to have a look at image 106 in your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's at English page 150; B/C/S page 149. All we need is one of the pictures on either -- thank you. Can we go down to the trees, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this picture that you took with a five-fold zoom, you also squashed it a bit so that the picture could fit within the indents of this page; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I fit it into this page, its dimensions that's for sure. This is a panoramic image, that is to say, it wasn't just one photographs that was taken. It was several photographs and then this panoramic image was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. But, Mr. Poparic, in point of fact when you look at that photo one might gain the impression that the growth you identify is immediately in front of a line of sight from the faculty of theology, but that's not the case at all, is it? There's a huge building separating this growth from the faculty of theology?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is this -- well, they used it as a kitchen down there. There was this lower building. Yes. It was zoomed in so then you lose this space between the person taking the photograph and the first thing that can be seen in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, the question is there is a huge building separating this growth from the faculty of theology. Not whether there was a kitchen somewhere or not. Do you agree that there was a building separating this growth from the faculty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- I mean, the interpretation I received ... I did not see any big buildings there. I said there is a building that is attached to this one. Perhaps it's about 4 or 5 metres high and that's the kitchen. So that building is there, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now let's go to -- let's move up in this page to your image 105 which you say is the faculty of theology at the end of the war. Now, you cropped this picture to show that there were -- to avoid showing that no trees blocked these openings that you see in the building, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. This is not my photograph. This is the photograph that I mentioned from that album that the head of this faculty showed us and allow us to take this picture. This was taken in 1996, and this is the other side. This is the entrance into the faculty of theology.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so you didn't crop this picture to put it in your report. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes. I mean, this picture just shows those openings where there were firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look, please, at 65 ter number 3336, which is an information report of a representative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you check the number, please. You mentioned only a four-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 33336. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's an information report from a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor who visited the faculty of theology in Nedzarici in October of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I want us -- and he attaches a number of photographs to his report and I want us to go to e-court page 10, please. Thank you. Now can we put that picture beside image 105 that we've just seen. Almost there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So here's the uncropped version of your image 105 and that shows that there are absolutely no trees blocking the line of sight from the faculty of theology. A contemporaneous photograph obtained from the faculty of theology contradicts you again. There's no trees.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, there are no trees but that does not refute what I stated. It only confirms it. And these openings are in the direction of - how I do put this? - towards the east, Alipasino Polje, not Dobrinja. That's what I said. There weren't any firing positions facing Dobrinja, rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- sorry [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... north-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a translation issue on page 42, line 21, and I didn't want to intervene because Mr. Poparic gave his answer. "And here we can find this is the second page." And actually he said, "This is the other side." And in B/C/S it sounds the same, "druga strana," so that's why it might create the confusion but now when he answered, I think the translators can confirm what I said and audio can be checked for this line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks for the correction, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we collapse image 105, please, and just go back to page 10 of 33336.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, this picture was taken in 1996. You don't see -- you don't see any trees blocking any part of the view from that building at that time in this photograph, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not see that in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 33336 receives exhibit number P7610, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to move on to a couple of incidents in another area of Sarajevo, and the first one is incident F-4. And the area is Hrasno. You talked in your report at English page -- in the section beginning at English page 97 and B/C/S page 100. That's at paragraphs 64 to 79. And in respect of this incident, you made the repeated assertion, referring to the evidence of the victim in this case, that no one had been hit by a sniper in that area and you made it your evidence in-chief, at transcript page 40466 and 40467, and I want to know something: Are you disputing the targeting of civilians in Hrasno by sniping.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing anything. I did not deal with this in any great detail. I just said what this witness had said. Namely, that to the best of her knowledge, not before or after that no one -- I mean, nothing more than that. Probably there were other casualties there, too. I think that I found in some documents that there were two or three people but near the Miljacka, the bridge, not this area. As far as I can remember. I came across such cases, but that is from other documents that are not related to this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But in point of fact, civilians living in the area of Hrasno in Bosnian-held Sarajevo were persistently targeted by sniping from SRK forces day after day after day. There was hardly a day that went by without some report of sniper fire. That's the fact of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you're claiming. I did not have any access to these documents, so I cannot confirm or deny anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's show you a document to see if it helps you towards some kind of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33073.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a war diary of the police station in Novo Sarajevo, and you can go over to the next page in both languages because the first page is just a title page. And it's a document that dates from March 1995 and it represents a compilation of reports on sniping and shelling incidents in Novo Sarajevo from February 1993 to February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over, please, to page 13 in B/C/S and page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you see in both languages halfway down the page, about halfway down the page, you see reference to the victims Nafa Taric and her daughter Elma who were residing in Srebrenicka Street being wounded on the 3rd of September, 1995. Pardon me, 1993. Now, I just want you to move forward -- and by the way she's not the only one who's wounded that day. Do you see reference to Munib Cutuk, the same entry. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then another person Envir Omerovic was wounded within 15 minutes of the same incident or the incident which wounded the Taric family. Now, look, Mr. Poparic, let's just go down in dates. That was on the 3rd of September. You see on the 4th of September, there's a report of Praga fire in the area of Hrasno. On the 5th, there's sniper fire from aggressor forces at Dolac Malta. On the 6th, there's another sniping incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over, please, in English to the next page, and we can stay on the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Poparic, almost every day during the month of September 1993 - and we can go over to the next page in B/C/S now as well - incidents of sniper fire in Hrasno were reported to the police. Sniping was constant. And now you've seen a document that confirms that. So on the basis of what you've just seen, are you prepared to accept constant sniping against civilians in Hrasno from February 1993 to February 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to accept something like that, I would have to have documents to analyse. Because I see here that you're showing a few pages, and then there's shelling and fire from small-arms. So there's the question what was intentional and what was unintentional. On the basis of this, I cannot say. It is a fact that there was shooting and that this fell on inhabited areas but whether this was intentional targeting of civilians, I cannot say on the basis of these two or three pages only.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, I didn't ask about whether or not this was intentional, and that's not your job. But you've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33073 receives exhibit number P7611, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the document is admitted into evidence. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you repeatedly in your testimony in-chief referred to the evidence of Mrs. Taric saying she claimed that there had been no sniper victims there and that she and her daughter were the first ones and you said that, as I had indicated earlier, at transcript page 40466. And then at 40467, you said, referring to Mrs. Taric, that she said that according to the knowledge she had, no one had been hit by a sniper in that area. And you also refer to them in your report at paragraph 76, saying or noting that Taric said that she and her daughter were the only ones who were shot in this area. But, in fact, in her witness statement, which you saw and you sourced in your footnotes 165 to 167 and 175, she says: "I never saw or heard that anybody was hit in that street." She doesn't say anything about area. And then she goes on to say in the very same paragraph that within one hour, five persons were hit by sniper fire in that area. You would agree that's what she says, right, because you saw that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree that she spoke of that area. As far as I can remember, she lived in that street and she knew. When you said -- well, she said about later when she was wounded and that can be seen here in this report that you showed, there were two or three other wounded persons but not in that street but in other locations. Maybe she meant them. And you read out yourself what she said, that until then, there hadn't been any persons hit in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what was read out, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to you have a look at what you sourced. It's 1D02925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, just to place on record that also P7610 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could we go to the next page in both languages. Let's see if I have the page references right. No, I have my page references incorrect. It's the next page. No, I have it, sorry. I apologise. Halfway through this page, page 2 in both languages, she said and I'll give you that: "I never saw or heard that anybody was in that street. We were the first and the last" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
