utterances.text: Was hit in that street.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Was hit in that street. We were the first and the last to be hit in that street. I know that because my husband is a military commander and he knows the details. I learned later, when I was in the hospital, that within one hour, five persons were hit by sniper fire ..." Oh, here she says "area." "In that area..." so my excuses -- sorry for earlier. "... in that area, but not in the street. These people were taken to the same hospital. This was ... reported on television." Now, before I deal with this document, I want to go to her Galic testimony, because you even referred to her Galic testimony in your evidence in-chief at transcript page 40469.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you, then, were aware that in her Galic testimony she was asked about this, and she said -- actually, let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32774; e-court page 61, please. If we go down to line 8, she says: "My husband didn't [sic] know about this. And the spot where my daughter and I were hit, wounded on that day, this was a safe line, a [sic] safe area to walk in. And this was where we went, not just us but other citizens of Sarajevo. We walked there safely in this particular location. And I'm talking about this location, I'm not talking about the next 20 metres to the left or to the right, or forwards" -- or, pardon me "backwards or forwards. I'm talking about that particular location, that spot. We were the only ones hit there. I'm not talking about the location where there were other cases, 15 metres from there, 15 to the left, 15 to the right, or 50 to the right."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You read her Galic testimony. You knew she had said this; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now let's go over to page 68. She speaks in page 68 about meeting and that's at line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Line 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Meeting the people who were shot in that area in the hospital, and she spoke with them. And she says, or she is asked at line 15: "Do you recall speaking about them, about the specific location where they were in relation to where you and your daughter were shot on that day? And she responds: "Yes." At line 19 she is asked: "Do you recall approximately how close to the location where you and your daughter were shot these other individuals were shot?" And she answered: "One lady, perhaps in the same direction in front, she was hit some 50 metres away from us. The other two individuals were to the right of that lady. But from our spot, they were approximately -- within a radius of 50 metres, I would say." So, here, again, the effect of your selective excerpting has been to try and create an impression that this might have been an isolated incident but the evidence of Mrs. Taric shows that the wounding of her and her daughter was just another incident in a protracted campaign. That's what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. In my report, I did not deal with whether that area was constantly targeted or not. I considered a specific case, and she specifically said that in the place where they were, nobody was wounded because there had been protective barriers. I did not deal with other cases that occurred outside of the barrier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you don't think that evidence of protracted sniping in the area of any one of these Scheduled Incidents is relevant to your analysis as a ballistics expert?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these specific cases, I don't have any such information. I analysed only one case. You cannot ascribe to me now other things. You can say there are so many people who were wounded in Sarajevo, and you didn't take them into account. No, I did not have information about other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please answer the question. Have you told us your little story. Can you now answer the question. Do you not take into account the incidents of sniping in the area in your analysis as a ballistic expert? That's the question. Yes or no. That's the -- if I must give you an idea how the question must be answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I have no data about these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not being asked about these cases. You're being asked about taking into account the number of incidents as a ballistic expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please have the statement of Nafa Taric at 1D02925 admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, my colleague is just pointing to me that to find out from you is this -- was this statement made for the purposes of Tribunal and does it have the normal attestation of a 92 ter or 92 bis statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me check. Your indulgence for a moment with respect to the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the meantime, we can MFI it, and you can come back to it, Madam Edgerton. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This was a -- this is a Defence upload, Your Honours, and we're having a look at it now and it looks like they might have only uploaded the first page. So what we'll do is come back to you on that after we've uploaded the full statement and the attestation which does exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That's why I was mentioning it. So, Madam Registrar, can give us a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D02925 receives exhibit number P7612, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the pages of the Galic testimony, 65 ter number 32774, e-court pages 61 and 68 and 69, which were the pages we spoke about in court, I'd like to have those admitted as the next Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I think you have read the relevant parts into the transcript. Could that suffice? Usually we don't admit transcript pages. Only -- we do that only if there's a specific reason, like we did, I think, this morning -- or yesterday about the marking we wanted to have on the -- on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can just note, Mr. President, my understanding is that expedient is useful and appropriate where the witness confirms the reading out of the material from the document. That is, you read from a transcript, the witness says, yes, I agree that's what was said at the time. So the tendering of the document then becomes superfluous because it's been affirmed by the witness. I just don't know if it happened in this case. And that's the only hesitation I think we have. So we can take a closer look and see if the basis for moving beyond the redundancy exists in the transcript, then the Court's point is well taken, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The pages are admitted, 32774, and may they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7613, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you have to upload the pages as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll MFI it until it's uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just one last point in relation to F-4. You said at -- in your report at English page 106, you said that you visited Ozrenska Street --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- and say that you were able to establish there was no optical visibility from the area toward the incident site. So here's what I want to know: Are you telling us when you say "no optical visibility," that you went to the assessed origin of fire identified by Mr. Van der Weijden and, from there, you yourself couldn't see the incident location?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there, marked by Mr. Van der Weijden as being at 829 metres from the place of the incident. And at the time when I was there, from the road - and I underline, from the road - I was not able to see it. That area has been developed a lot after the war. It's possible that Mr. Van der Weijden could see it in his own time, but I -- I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You didn't go to the location established by the GPS co-ordinates that Mr. Van der Weijden provided; right? Because you didn't have a GPS so you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could. You don't have to have a GPS. You can determine it using a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. All right --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's not correct that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where is a single photo from your personal inspection from the identical location that Mr. Van der Weijden visited to show that there's no line of sight to the place where the Taric family got shot? Where is a single photo?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took photos where something could be seen, not where there's nothing to see. I went through the whole area of the Ozrenska Street, and I was looking for visibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't have a single photo, so we're supposed to take your word for it that you can't see the incident location. That's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't take my word for it. In my report, I did not dispute that there was a view from this area to the place of the incident. There were about 10 or 15 metres where the trench was, there were photographs of the trench and I'm not disputing there was VRS firing position there, but I do dispute that the photograph made by Mr. Van der Weijden was taken from that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you said earlier that you don't take photographs where line of vision is not there. Yesterday we referred -- we were talking about another picture that you took in your report where you said the line of vision was obstructed by the garage. So you do take photographs where the line of vision is not there, according to you. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph that we looked at yesterday was not taken by me. It's a still from a video. I just marked the locations where the place of the incident was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in Ozrenska Street I have photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you cropped it into your report nonetheless. It make --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the photograph that we looked at yesterday. Is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another incident but I'll have to do that in private session, if we can, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Registrar, I note the time. We'll take a break and come back at quarter past 1.00. But before that, may the witness please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We adjourn. Come back at 15 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has been advised that the Prosecution has a preliminary matter they'd like to raise in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This morning we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Private session. May we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're sorry about that little inconvenience, Mr. Poparic. These are the vicissitudes of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we broke I omitted to tender the exhibit we had been dealing with, which is 65 ter 10027. If that could be admitted under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Edgerton. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives exhibit number P7614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. It is admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I want to move on, Mr. Poparic, to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, and one other additional administrative matter: The excerpted pages for P7613 have now been uploaded at 65 ter number 32744A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 32774A. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 32774A. Thank you very much. Madam Registrar, the MFI status can be removed and it can be admitted. You may proceed, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, in -- you talked in your testimony in-chief about the area of Marin Dvor at transcript pages 40392 to -93 and you described it in your report at paragraph 17 as the area stretching from the Sveti Josip church in the east to the outer limits of the Marsal Tito barracks in the west. Now that strip is about 500 metres long; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that strip of territory was frequently targeted by sniper fire. You accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just about the white sky-scrapers that you mentioned, and -- at transcript page 40392. Now, in your report, you said at paragraph 17a, pages 60 in English and 63 in B/C/S, that: "The sniper positions in the white sky-scrapers were obviously professionally constructed and aimed at the Marsal Tito barracks, since the view from these positions reached only as far as the technical school." But, because you referred to in your footnote 51, the forensic file that is P620, I'm sure you would agree with the following. Wherever you think -- so here's my question: Wherever you think the sniper positions might have been aimed, the white sky-scraper positions, those positions had a commanding view over territory past the technical school; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents that I have, that is not the case. There were some parts where it could be seen, others that were a bit more sheltered. The situation a bit more complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you prepared to agree that positions in these sky-scrapers had a view over territory that included the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you prepared to agree that the positions in the white sky-scrapers had a view over tram tracks, tram tracks in front of the barracks, in front of the Museum for Revolution, for two?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the barracks and the Museum of the Revolution, yes, yes, and the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, based on what you would have seen in P620, you would have seen that some of these positions had a view far west of Marsal Tito barracks. You saw that in the photographs that are part of P620. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I don't remember that I saw -- I mean, the Marsal Tito barracks is very big. I mean, I'm not sure. If you have this, you can show it to me. I can confirm -- I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said these positions reached only as far as the technical school, it wasn't quite accurate, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, about the technical school, I meant the area that is of interest from the point of view of those incidents that I dealt with. I mean, the sidewalk. I mean, it's not that precise, but I'm explaining now what it was that I meant and what led me to say that. So it was the sidewalk that was of interest to me, not the technical school, the Holiday Inn, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, what the photos in P620 show and P620 are - as I mentioned, are the forensic photos of these sniper positions - what these photos show is that every passing tram and pedestrian on Zmaja od Bosna could have been exposed to gunfire from SRK sniper positions in the white sky-scrapers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, wouldn't it be fair to the witness to show the photo instead of just referring to a P number of a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since he indicated that he can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem. Could we have a look at P620, please. Thank you. We could go to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that's a photo from a firing position at Grbavicka 8A and it was taken on 25th April, 1996, apartment 56 on the 14th floor. You can see the Holiday Inn. And you can see part of the national museum and you can see an area of Zmaja od Bosne in this photo, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that shows the view reached past the technical school, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is almost in front of the technical school. The technical school is right by this wall here -- well, if we're going to be precise, it extends a bit further but the difference is not significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You either accept it or you don't. This shows the view from the sniper positions reached east of the technical school, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. This is almost in front of the technical school. We can see very little.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at page 10. This is a picture that was taken from Grbavicka 8. This view shows an area along Zmaja od Bosne looking far west of the Marsal Tito barracks. You can see it. Do you agree with it, yes or no? Can you see that this photograph shows a view -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... just a minute. I can hardly see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- of Marsal Tito barracks along Zmaja od Bosne.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's that far away from the barracks. Although I cannot see it very well at all, but it's further from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at page 54. Ah, thank you for the enlargement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you recognise it now better, since it is enlarged. Can you now answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to identify ... I cannot locate it exactly. I'm a bit perplexed by these sky-scrapers, but it's further away from the Marsal Tito barracks. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go now to page 54.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a view from the 16th floor of Grbavicka 6, up Bulevar Borisa Kidrica Street and the Museum of the Revolution is immediately on the left-hand side. Do you agree that this shows -- this photo shows a view of tram tracks and pedestrian areas deep within Bosnian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We see the Museum of the Revolution here, the technical school, the Marsal Tito barracks, and opposite the technical school, this museum, this national museum.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I want to do one more and then I'm going to ask the same question I asked you earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the question was about tram tracks. The witness didn't respond to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh yes, part of the tram tracks can be seen in the street Zmaja od Bosne from the Museum of the Revolution to some place beyond the technical school. Then the tram tracks can be seen going down this street towards the railway station and to the left of the Museum of the Revolution, we see part of the tram tracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the pedestrian areas you were asked about? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are pedestrians paths. I don't know what the lady meant by "pedestrian areas." I mean, these are streets that had sidewalks along which pedestrians walked, and that can be seen. There's no denying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's do one more before we leave this. Let's go to page 64, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a view from a sniper position at Grbavicka 14a onto Bratstvo-Jedinstvo bridge. You can see it with the naked eye. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Orthodox church is further beyond. You can recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now do you accept that these photos show that every passing tram and pedestrian in the area could have been exposed to sniper fire from positions in these sky-scrapers?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were within the line of sight of any sniper shooter. But lest there be any confusion in this last photograph, there is no tram. This is across the Miljacka river so it's the border and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I didn't ask you that.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked about all photographs, and I'm saying about this one, that it's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This one, Madam Edgerton didn't refer to the tram tracks. She is just saying that people on that bridge are in the line of sight of the building where the snipers are alleged to have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you have for -- you have no idea from which floors fire in these buildings might have been opened in any of the incidents you examined. You have no idea; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that. There is no data supplied anywhere. The possibility was considered that it was from any floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But your analysis in almost every Scheduled Incident that's alleged to have taken place in this area depends on angle, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that angle differs depending on whether fire might have been opened from the second, the fourth, or the tenth floor, or the roof of any sniper position in these white sky-scrapers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to move onto to another building within this 500 metre stretch of territory, and that's the Metalka building. Now in your Karadzic testimony with respect to the Metalka building, we talked about firing positions, and you said: "If there's someone who said that, I will not dispute it, but we did not have such information which doesn't mean that no one included such information." That's at Karadzic transcript page 39188, lines 2 to 15; 65 ter number 32790, page 26. So, in the Karadzic case, you, as I understand you, didn't dispute the existence of SRK firing positions in the Metalka building, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither disputed it nor confirmed it, but I did my analysis as if they had been there. I took the allegations from the indictment and analysed the incident from that point of view. I don't have data to confirm that they were really there, and it doesn't matter for my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you don't exclude the possibility at all that SRK firing positions were located in the Metalka building, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not exclude that possibility and that's how I analysed the incidents. But whether they were really there, I can be of no assistance there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a military document related to perhaps this issue that may help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter number 12146.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- gezondheid. This is a document dated 3 September 1992 from the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command and if we go over to English page 4, B/C/S page 2, you see that the 1st pb, which I think is -- I think it's infantry company. Is defending the following front line: Metalka, left bank of the Miljacka river up to Strojorad, which is the right side of M. Djuraskovica Street into the depth of Rave Jankovica Street. So here's a contemporaneous military document that puts SRK forces defending the line of the Metalka building? You're not disputing that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's written.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 12146 receives Exhibit number P7615, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And it's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a statement from an UNMO in Sarajevo who was working in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 33352.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go over to page 3. This is the statement, ICTY statement of Muhamed Butt who was an UNMO in Sarajevo as part of the UNPROFOR contingent and an officer in the Pakistani army. Now in your language and in English the paragraph I want to direct to you is just the second one on this page, and I'll invite to you read it and I'll summarise. On the 5th of April, 1995, Mr. Butt described an incident where a French soldier for an anti-sniping team, positioned between the museum and the Holiday Inn, was shot by a sniper. Later it was confirmed by the French investigation team that there were all reasons to believe he was shot by a Serb sniper. "I was the incident," he writes, "in which the soldier was killed in the fork-lift. I came on site only seven to ten minutes after the incident." And then he goes on, saying, "Normally I wasn't supposed to investigate civilians in which UN personnel were involved, but I got a message that a civilian was hit. When I came to the scene together with a Jordanian colleague and we were fired at too." At that moment when they began their investigation, the two APCs that were on-site fled away. And Mr. Butt and his colleague had to say one to hour to hour and a half under fire due to the continuous sniping in their direction. He could see the fire was coming from Bosnian-Serb-held positions. He was even able to give his colleagues on the Lima side the precise location of the sniper. He was positioned in what they called the Metalka building. So my question to you is: Now do you accept that SRK firing positions were really in the Metalka building?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not sufficient evidence for me. It's a statement from an observer. He doesn't say whether his colleagues from Lima had gone to Metalka, whether they found something, he doesn't say what indicated that the fire came from Metalka. There are not sufficient elements for me to conclude that it was really the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, and I think I may have misread this. This incident is the 15th of April, not the 5th of April. Right. So evidence that somebody was under fire for an hour to an hour and a half from the Metalka building doesn't convince you that there were Serb firing positions there. That's what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying there are not sufficient elements here for me to conclude. He doesn't mention his colleagues. He was the only one who noticed it was from Metalka. Maybe it's true, but maybe ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You answered my question and you said no. Let's move on. I want to talk about a sniping incident that you address in your report, and it's incident F-8, and it appears on sections that begin at pages 156 in English, 155 in B/C/S, and paragraphs 133 to 146. Now this is a tram-sniping incident that happened on the 19th of June, 1994. And just before we start, I just want to ask you one question: Do you accept that trams packed with civilians are not military targets?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good. Now this incident, in this incident, there were a number of wounded while travelling in a tram which was going west on Zmaja od Bosna towards Alipasino Polje and the tram was near the Holiday Inn at the time of the incident. So you accept that this happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you try to show that the shot that hit this tram couldn't have come from SRK positions for a couple of reasons, and I just want to talk about two of the -- the main ones. First of all, you rely on a single video still from a report by Aernout van Lynden which was recorded in 1992, and that's at paragraph 142, and that report is P77, by the way. So you rely on this report, and you say: "According to the report of the Sky News reporter, Aernout van Lynden, the Army of Republika Srpska position at the Jewish cemetery wasn't a sniper position as the soldier was armed with a simple M70, 7.62-millimetre automatic rifle." Putting aside completely whether this meets your personal definition of what a sniping position should be, this soldier could have fired that type of rifle from that position; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have, but the police established that it was a 7.9-millimetre bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask you that. I want to play this video, this clip, and it's not a very -- it's not a long one, at all, Your Honours. It's about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The image that was on the screen just now, you didn't give us the 65 ter number for it. I'm not quite sure what you intend doing with it. At some stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that was just his report, Your Honours, with those paragraphs, and I think the status of that report and whether or not it will be broadcast are still to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we're going to play now P77, and I'm going to pause this at a couple of places. It's going to play from time code -- begins at time code 11:34.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll play the whole clip and I'm going pause at a couple of places.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "... to an elderly Serb neighbour. "The Convent of the Sisters of the Little Jesus is one of the very few havens in the area which even for Sarajevo standards is notorious for the ferocity of its war. "The no man's land that's given the area its name is the Jewish cemetery. Across the jumble of graves new and old some of the fiercest battles have been fought. The string of little villas lining the cemetery have been turned into bunkers, sitting room walls roughly redecorated with lines of logs, although some of the defences are more imaginative. Bathroom mirrors subtly deployed to allow one guard to view all angles. Of late the tanks against the Serb lines in this sector have diminished, leaving the battalion commander exuding confidence. "We are ready for a long struggle, but we believe we'll only spend a short time in these positions. Either they'll have to accept peace or there will be an all out war in which we'll try to achieve victory in a very short time. "The major's confidence is understandable. Unlike his opponents, he does not face a lack of logistical support made worse by siege. And if he is ordered to attack he will do so from a commanding position. So commanding that in the streets below, few dare to move. Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Having seen this video that you refer to in your report, you would agree that there is absolutely nothing here to indicate that this is the only SRK firing position in the area of the Jewish cemetery; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But this just an illustration of where the Jewish cemetery was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. You've answered my question. There's also no evidence here that suggests that every SRK position in the area had the identical views to the view you have included in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And surely you would acknowledge that just because one camera shot viewed through one gun opening might show a tree partially obstructing a view doesn't mean that every SRK shooting position had the same view as that one?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your report, you also discuss how if the bullet in this incident came from the Jewish cemetery, it would have struck the tram more or less at a right angle and then, as I understand your argument, you try and show that the bullet didn't strike the tram at a right angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we could go to image 115, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English page 160; B/C/S page 158. Right. It's just to see the photo so we could just deal with one image.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here at image 115 you've got this photo of a hole in the exterior of the tram - right? - next to a photo of the hole inside the tram - right? - and then if we can go over to image 116 on the next page, please, then here you extrapolate where you think the bullet would have entered the interior of the tram. And you say just beneath the photo the dotted red circle - right? - marks the point where the projectile exited the paneling on the inner side as assumed on the basis of image 115. So that's all this is; right? Just your assumptions of where the interior hole would be; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Below the picture, it says putative location. It's not an exact value. That's not what the conclusion was based on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Let's go over one image to image 117 because there, you also try to extrapolate the angle of entry from the shape of the bullet-hole in the exterior paneling. So how do you this, is you make a really big enlargement of the hole and then you use this computer programme to do a measurement of the hole's diameter from different positions. That's what you do; right? Just yes or no, is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all I asked. Is that a fair summary of what you do?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I can explain how it's done because it's important. I cannot answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly so, but partly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Without getting into your methodology, you don't have a single citation to any ballistics literature about enlarging the image of the hole and using a computer programme to do a relative measurement of the hole's diameter. You ... do you? You don't cite anything to support your methodology. So -- is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for me to cite. These are the general principles of applied geometry which I studied at depth at school. It's pure geometry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, since you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, since you're talking about geometry, my question is: You didn't have any concerns about how pixilated and grainy this enlargement was when you were using it for the basis of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see for yourself that it's not of great influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, whether Madam Edgerton can see for herself or not, is immaterial. She wants you to answer the question that she put to you. Will you please answer that question? Otherwise, if -- things we can see for ourselves, we wouldn't have called you as a witness. Will you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, it was not a problem for me. The pixilation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Even if a bullet enters at hole at a perfect 90-degree tangent in every direction, that doesn't mean the hole is going to be perfectly round, does it? Any slight imperfection or weakness in the middle of the panel could cause an irregular tear.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The speed of the projectile is such and the homogeneity of the material is also very high. So it's out of the question. The best example is glass.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- when it pierces the glass, the velocity is such that the glass is not shattered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's your basis for your assertions now about the homogeneity of the material? You've admitted to conducting this analysis on the basis of photographs. You've not done a material analysis, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do the analysis of the material but I know how that material is obtained, and how it's manufactured. It's obtained by rolling. You get a perfectly homogeneous material.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And even if we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know when and where this tram was constructed and manufactured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were produced in Czechoslovakia, it was at the time, around 1980 or a few years earlier or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is common knowledge but what do you know exactly about the manufacturing of such a part of the tram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That tram on the exterior is made of metal, steel. Inside there is isolation, styrofoam and another layer of some artificial material. I don't know what it is. I don't know exactly how I could call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you visit a factory where this was produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't. I just saw trams that were damaged so I saw what it looks like, how that surface was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said in this way you get a perfectly homogeneous material. What is the basis for this conclusion? What factual basis do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The factual basis is that I worked such material quite a bit and I know how this is made. In steel mills, the steel is rolled so you get this perfect material, perfectly homogenous material. It's not that somewhere it is weaker and in other places that it is stronger, and, of course, there is quality control and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I stop you. Do you know anything about quality control in the Czechoslovakian factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that factory I mean, you're referring to the tram factory or in steel mills as such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not in any steel mill of the world. The steel mill where the metal was produced and used for trams. We're talking only about that. Do you have any information about the quality checks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have information on quality control for sheeting. Factories of trams buy that in the market so I have that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm only asking about trams, the material produced for trams, produced in Czechoslovakia. I take it from your answer you don't have a factual basis especially not about quality control; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly. A tram factory buys sheets from steel mills at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... general information how it is done somewhere in the world. I'm talking about this kind of trams and the material used in the factory in Czechoslovakia. You are not answering my question, I think we are at the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been trying to finish this one incident so we wouldn't have to go back to it so I've stretched my time. My colleague has asked for a few minutes, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How few, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have stretched the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before I let you do that, didn't you want to -- have you rounded off your questioning on this point? Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can deal with it tomorrow very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President -- Thank you, Your Honour. I was trying to follow through on some housekeeping matters while Ms. Edgerton attended to cross-examination duties. The first is the following: The Court MFI'd P7613 pending its uploading as a separate document. I can report that it has now been uploaded as 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have dealt with that already and it's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies. Then the other -- then it's even quicker than two minutes. The other issue was that the Trial Chamber MFI'd P7612 after Ms. Edgerton advised the Trial Chamber that she or we would get back to the Court on whether it had an attestation, since only one page had been uploaded. And I can report that the entirety has now been uploaded as 65 ter 33376 including the signed acknowledgment page and would therefore ask that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 33376, 65 ter and ask that to be admitted as P7612.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will you please remove the MFI status to P7612 and it's now admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Poparic, we've come to the end of the day. Just to remind that you have you not finished with your testimony and therefore you are not allowed to speak to anybody about your testimony, whether given or still to be given, and not anybody. Not any person at all. If you remember that, you are excused and you may follow the usher. Do you want to talk before he leaves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly because you ordered me to get back on this Rule 70. My learned friend, Mr. Tieger, was right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should we --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Private session --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rule 70 does not apply. It was imposed by the party not by the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it by Court, or by the party who ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By the party. It was not imposed by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but the Rule 70 is normally imposed by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it would be clear, if I understand it correctly, it was imposed by the party or by the witness rather than the provider. And there is no real provider in this instance I think is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That clarifies it. Thank you very much. Is that all? Okay. We then stand adjourned and we'll sit tomorrow, Wednesday, 4th of November, 2015, 9.30 in the morning, in the same room, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of November, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 25
